title: Jensen Huang Is Back. Nvidia’s (NVDA) Bull Case Remains
detail:

Jensen Huang is back at the helm, and Nvidia's (NVDA) bull case remains in play. Nvidia shares surged 31.5% on November 23 after news of Jensen Huang's reinstatement, underscoring how closely investor confidence in the company is tied to its co-founder.

While near-term volatility is likely to persist, I remain decisively Bullish over the long term. Nvidia makes the chips, networking gear, and software powering the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and its earnings story is strong enough to ride out the ups and downs.

Huang's Return Restores Continuity, but Not Trust

Huang's return restores strategic continuity, but it does not restore trust overnight. Nvidia disclosed on November 12 that its co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) had resigned after the board accepted his resignation on November 11. The stock finished that session 4.3% lower. On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang had been reinstated, and the shares rose 31.5%.

The episode highlighted a degree of key-person risk that I had underestimated. Nvidia's product cadence and customer confidence have always been closely tied to Huang. His return obviously removes the immediate succession problem. However, it leaves investors with a governance question.

The board reinstated him before completing its independent investigation, shortly after creating a National Security and Export Control Committee on November 17 and alongside launching a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Those oversight steps are the right moves, but they do not excuse reversing a major leadership decision before the facts are settled.

For my Bullish thesis, Huang's return is a stabilizer, though stronger governance is still required.

Nvidia's Earnings Still Point to Powerful AI Demand

Nvidia's results still point to very strong AI demand, and that's the part of the argument I find most compelling. Q3 FY2027 revenue was up 103% year-over-year to $115.8 billion, and Data Center revenue was up 110% to $107.6 billion. GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $2.70. Management has guided to around $130 billion in Q4 FY2027 revenue, plus or minus 3%, all the way through the end of the year, despite assuming zero Data Center compute revenue from China.

Nvidia's product roadmap also gives me confidence the company can sustain growth. The company has started shipping Vera Rubin NVL72, with systems already operating at major cloud partners. This comes as some of its biggest customers continue to invest heavily in AI infrastructure. Meta (META), Google (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN) all raised their capital spending plans during their October earnings updates, suggesting that demand for the computing infrastructure Nvidia provides could remain strong.

title: AMD vs. ASML: As Wall Street Questions the AI Boom, Which Chip Stock Wins in 2027?
detail:
AMD vs. ASML: As Wall Street Questions the AI Boom, Which Chip Stock Wins in 2027?
RJ Fulton, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 8:46 AM PST 6 min read
AMD
ASML
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A wave of selling across the semiconductor industry has raised questions about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, prompting investors to reassess valuations and long-term growth prospects. Among the companies caught in the downturn is Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and ASML Holding (NASDAQ:ASML).

As of November 25, AMD shares had fallen approximately 38% from their 52-week high, while ASML had declined roughly 35%. Despite these losses, both remain critical to AI infrastructure. AMD designs advanced processors for data centers, while ASML supplies the specialized equipment needed to manufacture cutting-edge chips.

With both stocks trading well below their recent highs, which offers the more compelling combination of growth potential, competitive advantages, and valuation heading into 2027?

The case for Advanced Micro Devices

AMD is a leading semiconductor designer specializing in high-performance processors for data centers and consumer computing. Its portfolio includes graphics processing units (GPUs), server processors, and adaptive computing technologies. The company's expanding presence in AI infrastructure represents a significant growth opportunity as technology companies invest heavily in computing capacity.

Financial performance has been strong. For the 12 months ended September 26, 2026, AMD generated approximately $45.4 billion in revenue, representing year-over-year growth of 41.9%. Net income reached approximately $7.6 billion, equivalent to a net profit margin of 16.7%, reflecting growing demand for its data center and computing products.

AMD also maintains a strong balance sheet, with a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.1 and a current ratio of 2.9 as of December 2025. During fiscal 2025, the company generated approximately $6.7 billion in free cash flow, providing flexibility to invest in product development and expand its AI computing business. However, stock-based compensation represented approximately 21% of operating cash flow, an important consideration when evaluating the company's underlying cash generation.

The case for ASML

ASML occupies a unique position in the semiconductor industry as the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems used to manufacture the world's most advanced chips. Its technology is essential to leading semiconductor manufacturers, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM), Samsung Electronics (OTC:SSNLF), and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), providing ASML with a significant competitive advantage and broad exposure to growing demand for advanced computing.

title: Not AMD. This Is the 1 Company Nvidia Should Worry About Most.

Not AMD. This Is the 1 Company Nvidia Should Worry About Most.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 9:35 AM PST 4 min read
NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors have had a rough go recently. First, the stock wasn't being fully valued due to skepticism about AI spending. Then, its co-founder was forced to resign as CEO. Even though Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia on Nov. 23, shares are down 18% this year and more than 35% from its all-time highs.

That's certainly a cause for concern, and one competitor that is looking to gain ground is AMD (NASDAQ:AMD). AMD also makes GPUs that are direct competitors to Nvidia's products, and is looking to capitalize on Nvidia's missteps.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But, regardless of who makes the GPU, they have the same limitations. There's one Nvidia competitor out there that's taking a different approach and is the one investors should fear most: Broadcom(NASDAQ:AVGO).

Image source: Getty Images.

Broadcom's custom AI chips are gaining traction

I think Broadcom is better positioned than AMD to capture market share. AMD makes GPUs like Nvidia, but they have a fundamental problem: they're not specifically designed for anything. GPUs have incredible performance and can process multiple calculations in parallel, but being good at all things means they're not great at one thing in particular. In many settings, these computing devices only see one type of workload during their service life. That's wasted potential, and using a computing unit specifically designed for that workload could result in huge cost savings.

That's exactly the idea Broadcom is running with, as it's developing application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) with several partners. The most prominent example of Broadcom's work is Alphabet's (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). These devices have allowed Google to construct one of the most cost-efficient computing infrastructures available, and other companies like Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) have utilized these devices. Furthermore, Alphabet is selling TPUs to outside companies like Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), which shows just how popular these units are becoming.

This is a major threat to Nvidia's empire, because custom AI units offer better computing value than its GPUs. While GPUs will never be fully replaced because they have several uses, as custom AI chips from Broadcom improve, so will the number of workloads they can tackle.

title: Here’s Why I’d Still Buy Nvidia Over AMD With or Without Jensen Huang at CEO.
detail:
Here’s Why I’d Still Buy Nvidia Over AMD With or Without Jensen Huang at CEO.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 8:05 AM PST 5 min read
NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) are rivals. These companies compete in multiple industries, but none as big as data centers right now. Both AMD and Nvidia have strong product offerings. Still, Nvidia took an early lead due to having better software, and that was all it took for Nvidia's product lineup to become the go-to in the data center industry.

However, Nvidia's investment thesis recently hit a bump in the road due to issues involving co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Huang resigned due to misconduct issues, but was reinstated by the board a few days later.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But Huang isn't out of the woods yet, as he must testify before Congress about recent events. This could cause a distraction, and Nvidia's issues undoubtedly give AMD an advantage right now/

But I still don't think it's even close to enough to consider investing in AMD over Nvidia.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia's data center business is larger and growing at a faster rate

The best way to compare these two stocks is to look at how their respective data center businesses are doing. This offers a more direct comparison and reveals to investors how each is doing in the most important sector.

AMD and Nvidia's third quarters don't end at the same time. AMD operates on a calendar-year fiscal schedule, with its Q3 ending on Sept. 30. Nvidia's is shifted 13 months forward, with its fiscal 2027 Q3 ending on Oct. 25, so a perfect comparison isn't possible. Still, it's the best investors have.

AMD's data center revenue grew in Q3 at a 97% pace to $8.5 billion. Those are strong results, but they fall well short of Nvidia's. During its fiscal 2027 third quarter, Nvidia's data center revenue totaled $107.6 billion, up 110% compared to a year ago. So, not only is Nvidia far larger, but it's also growing appreciably faster. Those two factors are rarely combined, which is what makes Nvidia so dominant.

However, all those results were obtained before the issues surrounding Huang and China export concerns came to light. While some may think this will affect Nvidia's growth and sales, I'm not sure it will. The reality is that the AI hyperscalers cannot get their hands on as much computing power as they want right now. So, regardless of who is selling the computing unit to them, they want it. As a result, AMD's and Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are practically selling themselves. This is a great place to be, and Nvidia will likely be able to ride out the status quo it established until the situation gets a bit more under control.
